title: A Circular Queue of Fixed Size

concept.title: An array that wraps around
body: A queue with a **fixed capacity** `k` can live in an array of size `k`. If you always put new items at the end and remove from the front, the used part of the array would slide to the right and run out of room, even if the front part is empty. The solution: let the indexes **wrap around** with the modulo operator, as on a clock.
Keep `head` (the index of the front item) and `size` (the number of items). The next free place is `(head + size) % k` and the last item is at `(head + size - 1) % k`.

body.code:
enqueue x: if size == k: fail
           buf[(head + size) % k] = x; size += 1
dequeue:   if size == 0: fail
           head = (head + 1) % k; size -= 1
front:     buf[head]  if size > 0 else -1
rear:      buf[(head + size - 1) % k]  if size > 0 else -1

body: This structure is called a **circular buffer** or ring buffer. It is used wherever a fixed amount of recent data must be kept, such as audio buffers and network packets.

statement: Implement a queue that holds at most `k` numbers. Process `n` operations (each line has an operation and a number; the number is ignored except for `enQueue`). `enQueue x` adds `x` at the back and prints `yes`, or prints `no` if the queue is full. `deQueue` removes the front and prints `yes`, or prints `no` if the queue is empty. `Front` and `Rear` print the first and last number, or -1 if the queue is empty. `isEmpty` and `isFull` print `yes` or `no`. Print one line for every operation.
inputFormat: Each of the next `n` lines has an operation and a number.

examples.input:
6 2
enQueue 1
enQueue 2
enQueue 3
Rear 0
isFull 0
deQueue 0
examples.note: The third enQueue fails (no), Rear is 2, the queue is full (yes), and deQueue works (yes).

hints: Use an array of size k with `head` and `size`.
The next free place is `(head + size) % k`.
Check `size == k` before adding and `size == 0` before removing or reading.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, k = map(int, input().split())
ops = [input().split() for _ in range(n)]

# Your code here

explanation: The queue lives in an array of size `k`; `head` and `size` describe it and the indexes wrap around with `% k`, so freed places at the front are reused.
